findings.body:
`InsecureSkipVerify: true` is hard-coded on the shared `NewClient()` transport with no environment, build-tag, or config gate. Every consumer of this client — including production — will accept any certificate (or no valid chain), enabling MITM on ledger traffic.

The staging self-signed cert note and TICKET-77 do not constrain runtime behavior. Keep verification enabled by default; only skip (or prefer: trust the staging CA / custom `RootCAs`) when an explicit non-prod signal is set, and refuse to start prod with skip enabled.

```suggestion
		Transport: &http.Transport{
			TLSClientConfig: &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12},
		},
```

If staging still needs a temporary bypass, gate it explicitly (e.g. `if cfg.AllowInsecureTLS && cfg.Env == "staging"`) and never default it on.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this unconditionally disables TLS certificate verification for every ledger HTTP client, including production.

## Narrative

`NewClient()` now always installs `tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true}`. The comment mentions a self-signed staging cert and TICKET-77, but nothing in the code limits the bypass to staging. Any caller of `NewClient()` inherits a transport that accepts arbitrary certificates, so a network-path attacker can MITM ledger traffic (credentials, account movements, PII) in every environment that uses this client.

A ticket and a "revisit before prod" comment are not a control. Gate the skip on an explicit staging/dev signal (or better: ship the staging CA / pin the cert), keep verification on by default, and fail closed in production.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: NewClient() hard-codes tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true} with only a comment/TICKET note and no env, build-tag, or config gate; the base version used a plain http.Client with normal verification. Any consumer of this shared factory will skip cert validation and be exposed to MITM.
